## TL;DR

The review was right: the earlier handoff image showed a loading resource panel and did not prove the process table at 375px. I replaced the unstable capture data with a preview-only Control fixture that pins one process and a short history for both resource sparklines. The populated resource panel now has declared desktop and phone captures, and Playwright exercised empty usage/activity plus usage and decision service failures at both viewport widths. The existing narrow-screen table fix is now covered by both geometry and component fixture tests.

## Work and rationale

The underlying layout fix was already present when I resumed: the process table wrapper scrolls horizontally, and its six-column header and rows keep a 560px minimum width. The test suite had a responsive geometry test, but the UI handoff evidence did not show the same thing. The actual issue was capture reliability. The first capture could land before system resource data arrived, and the old synthetic geometry test could not prove the component rendered a process.

I added `system:processTable` as a named preview fixture. It supplies plausible machine and repository metrics plus one task-linked process row. This makes the process table deterministic for the Mission Control screenshots without relying on which processes happen to exist on the capture host. The resource component seeds a two-point CPU and memory history only for this fixture, so the sparklines render immediately in the capture and the screenshot does not wait for repeated live sampling. A component test mounts `SystemResourcePanel`, applies the fixture, and checks the rendered row, runtime column, and both chart paths.

I updated the QA record to describe the responsive behavior and the evidence gathered in headless Playwright. At 1280px the table columns fit in the resource panel. At 375px the panel stacks its metrics while the table keeps its own horizontal scroll area; the page document remains 375px wide. The usage and decision requests were intercepted with 503 responses to exercise their visible error messages at both viewport widths. The dashboard also showed its empty usage and live activity copy with all six status cards present.

## Approaches tried

I first used live server resource samples. That produced a populated desktop panel, but the phone capture still sometimes showed the waiting state. I then added a selector screenshot for the resource panel, which captures content below the fold, and a deterministic fixture so the table can be present before the capture begins. I also checked the generated PNG dimensions and opened the resource-panel captures to confirm the phone view contains the horizontally clipped table inside the panel rather than a widened page.

For failure states I used Playwright route interception instead of editing application state. This lets the normal dashboard components receive service errors and display their actual Retry and error copy. The browser run recorded no page errors, and document width matched the requested viewport at both sizes.

## Challenges and blockers

The app loads the resource stream asynchronously, and the six-column table sits below several vertically stacked metrics on a phone. A normal viewport screenshot therefore proved neither that the table had loaded nor that its narrow scroller worked. Capturing the resource panel element, combined with a stable fixture, solved both problems while keeping the viewport at 375px. The CPU and memory lines also depend on having more than one sample; the fixture now supplies that small history directly.

No human device, account, or external service was needed. Browser verification stayed headless and used the auth-less server from a scratch clone of this task worktree.

## Key learnings

Responsive evidence should capture the component that owns the overflow, not just the page’s first viewport. A narrow table can be correct even when its full width is wider than the device, as long as the scroller contains that width and the document does not inherit it. Tests should therefore check both sides of the contract: the table’s minimum readable width and the wrapper’s containment within the viewport.

Preview fixtures are also useful for visual QA when live server samples are nondeterministic. Pinning the actual resource component inputs made the screenshots repeatable and let a component test protect the specific content that the reviewer asked to see. The final handoff check result will be appended after the scoped RepoOS check completes.
